name: vvdec
why: Fraunhofer's H.266/VVC decoder is a fascinating look at a modern video codec, though it is mostly a library.

brief.what_it_is: VVdeC is Fraunhofer HHI's software decoder for H.266/VVC (Versatile Video Coding), written as a C library with a sample command-line app, vvdecapp. It takes raw VVC bitstreams (NAL units) and outputs decoded frames. The app writes raw YUV or YUV4MPEG2 (y4m) files: yuv420p10le for 10-bit input and yuv420p for 8-bit. It can also write to stdout for piping. The README describes it as a fast decoder that supports all features of the VVC Main10 profile. The homepage says it is resource efficient, multithreaded, and capable of live decoding up to 4Kp60.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no separate motivation. The homepage presents it as Fraunhofer HHI's open-source reference-quality decoder for the new VVC standard, which it says achieves about 50% bit-rate reduction over H.265/HEVC at the same subjective quality. The paired encoder, VVenC, is listed alongside it.
brief.how_it_works: The decoder is passed one NAL unit at a time in an access unit, through vvdec_decode(). It returns VVDEC_TRY_AGAIN when it needs more data, or VVDEC_OK with a decoded frame. Remaining frames are drained with vvdec_flush() until VVDEC_EOF. Decoding runs on a thread pool sized by --threads, with 0 meaning single-threaded in the main thread and -1 meaning one thread per core.

brief.install_notes: Requires CMake. The GNU Make wrapper is optional. Build options are documented on the Wiki Build page, which I did not fetch. For WebAssembly you need the Emscripten SDK installed, activated and on PATH. Conformance bitstreams are not downloaded unless you pass enable-bitstream-download=1. Homebrew is not mentioned in the README, so the brew formula's packaging is outside what I read.
brief.standout: It is a software decoder that aims to decode VVC live, including 4K at 60 fps, and it compiles to WebAssembly so it can run in a browser. The README also cites the ICIP 2020 paper on the live-decoder design.
brief.status: Unknown from the pages I read. The README's copyright runs to 2026, and it mentions version v0.1.2.0 as a fix. The usage wiki page was last edited 10 Oct 2024. I did not check release tags or the last commit date.
brief.caveats: The README claims full support only for the VVC Main10 profile. Platform support is partial: the table marks Win32, macOS x86_64 and armv7 on Windows as not tested or not working, and Safari WASM as not working. The wiki's usage page labels the standalone vvdecapp app as deprecated, though the README still lists it as the main way to run the decoder. The README leaves licensing to LICENSE.txt, which I did not read. The wiki's single-threaded note says --threads 1 can still use more than one core. The homepage is a German-language institute page that links out to GitHub, and it carries no install or usage instructions of its own.
quotes: VVdeC, the Fraunhofer Versatile Video Decoder, is a fast software H.266/VVC decoder implementation supporting all features of the VVC Main10 profile.
Fraunhofer HHI has developed a resource efficient, multithreaded VVC software decoder that enables live decoding up to 4Kp60 ultra high resolution video.
The application can be used to decompress raw VVC bitstreams into y4m or raw YUV files.

judge.reason: VVdeC makes the relatively obscure H.266/VVC standard tangible: decode real bitstreams and explore a codec promising roughly half HEVC’s bitrate, beyond generic media plumbing.

entry.title: vvdec
entry.tldr: Fraunhofer's open-source H.266/VVC video decoder: feed it a raw next-generation bitstream and get plain YUV frames back, with a library underneath.
entry.deeper_look:
vvdec is Fraunhofer HHI's software decoder for H.266/VVC (Versatile Video Coding), the successor to H.265/HEVC. It is a C library with a small command-line app, vvdecapp, that reads a raw VVC bitstream and writes decoded frames as raw YUV or YUV4MPEG2 (y4m). It can also write to stdout, so it fits into a pipe. The project says it supports all features of the VVC Main10 profile.

The homepage presents it as a reference-quality, open-source decoder for a standard that claims about 50% bit-rate reduction over HEVC at the same subjective quality. The README gives no other motivation. A paired encoder, VVenC, is listed alongside it, and the README shows decoded output piped straight into that encoder's app.

The interesting part is how a codec looks from the inside. The library API is small: you hand it one NAL unit at a time through vvdec_decode(). It answers VVDEC_TRY_AGAIN until it has a full picture, then VVDEC_OK with a frame, and vvdec_flush() drains what is left. Decoding runs on a thread pool sized by --threads. The authors cite an ICIP 2020 paper on the live-decoder design, and they say it can decode 4Kp60 in real time. It also builds to WebAssembly for the browser.

The door here is the structure of modern video: bitstreams, NAL units, access units, and frames reconstructed from them. You need a VVC file to try it on, since the README does not point to a ready-made sample.
entry.install:
brew install vvdec
You also need a raw VVC bitstream (.266 or similar) to decode. To build from source instead, you need CMake; the WebAssembly build needs the Emscripten SDK.

Decodes a raw VVC file into a YUV4MPEG2 file, chosen by the .y4m extension.
Streams decoded frames into the separate VVenC encoder app to re-encode them. vvencapp is not part of this project.

entry.whats_unique: It is an open decoder for a very new codec that aims at live 4K60 decoding on the CPU, and it compiles to WebAssembly so it can run in a browser.
entry.caveats: Full support is claimed only for the Main10 profile, some platforms are marked untested or not working, and the wiki labels the standalone vvdecapp app as deprecated in favour of the library.
